claims.text: The agreement is dated London, 3 January 1919, and was signed by Amir Faisal for the Arab Kingdom of Hejaz and by Dr Chaim Weizmann for the Zionist Organisation.
Article II provided that after the Peace Conference 'the definite boundaries between the Arab State and Palestine shall be determined by a Commission' agreed by the parties.

Article III required Palestine's constitution and administration to afford 'the fullest guarantees for carrying into effect the British Government's Declaration of the 2nd of November, 1917' (the Balfour Declaration).

Article IV stated that 'all necessary measures shall be taken to encourage and stimulate immigration of Jews into Palestine on a large scale', while protecting the rights of Arab peasant and tenant farmers.

Article V guaranteed free exercise of religion and Article VI provided that 'the Mohammedan Holy Places shall be under Mohammedan control'; Article IX referred disputes to the British Government for arbitration.

Faisal's appended reservation (in the translation printed by UNISPAL) made his concurrence conditional: 'Provided the Arabs obtain their independence as demanded in my Memorandum dated the 4th of January, 1919'; otherwise the agreement would be 'void and of no account or validity'.
The Jewish Virtual Library's text of the agreement, including the reservation, gives as its source George Antonius, The Arab Awakening (1938), pp. 437–439.

Faisal and Weizmann first met in June 1918 at Faisal's camp in Transjordan; according to minutes by Lt Col P. C. Joyce, Faisal 'personally accepted the possibility of future Jewish claims to territory in Palestine' but said only his father could make political commitments.

In a letter to Felix Frankfurter dated 3 March 1919, written from the Hejaz delegation in Paris, Faisal called the Zionist proposals 'moderate and proper' and wrote that Arabs 'will wish the Jews a most hearty welcome home'.
At San Remo in April 1920 the Allies assigned Syria and Lebanon to France and Iraq and Palestine to Britain; after the battle of Maysalun on 24 July 1920 Faisal's Damascus government ended.
A EuroClio history-education article (Bob Stradling, 2019) concludes that the Allied allocation of Syria to France made the agreement 'null and void as far as Faisal was concerned'.
In 1947, according to Rick Richman, Weizmann told the United Nations that Faisal's condition (independence for Arab territories outside Palestine) had been fulfilled.

The UN study 'Origins and Evolution of the Palestine Problem' quotes Faisal's 1 January 1919 memorandum ('In Palestine, the enormous majority of the people are Arabs') and argues he 'in no manner consented to the establishment of a Jewish State'.
In July 1919 the Syrian Congress rejected French claims, claimed Palestine as part of Syria and opposed Jewish immigration.

disputes.question: Did the agreement ever take effect, and was Faisal's condition met?

positions.view: Lapsed / void: Faisal's condition (Arab independence per his 4 January 1919 memorandum) was not met once France took Syria in 1920, so by its own terms the agreement was void.

Fulfilled in substance: Weizmann told the UN in 1947 that the condition (independence of Arab lands outside Palestine) had been met; this reading is used by pro-Zionist writers to present the agreement as evidence of early Arab acceptance.

Limited scope: the UN study argues Faisal never consented to a Jewish state, and Palestinian Arab bodies (e.g. the 1919 Syrian Congress) rejected Zionist claims, so the agreement did not bind Palestinian Arabs.
UNISPAL/JVL (Antonius-derived) translation: agreement 'deemed void and of no account or validity' if any departure occurs.
EuroClio renders it: 'If changes are made I cannot be answerable for failing to carry out this agreement' — a softer formulation.

entries.topic: Muslim-Christian Associations, the Palestine Arab Congresses and the Arab Executive, 1918–1923

claims.text: Muslim-Christian Associations were formed at the end of 1918 to present a united Palestinian front and grew into a body with branches in many towns.

Muslim-Christian Societies were organised in Palestine's leading towns in 1917–1920, pressed the Peace Conference and Britain to repeal the Balfour Declaration and called for a united Syria; the British military administration encouraged their establishment.

In November 1918 Islamic-Christian associations organised counter-demonstrations against the first-anniversary celebrations of the Balfour Declaration; Jerusalem mayor Musa Kazim al-Husseini led a demonstration on 3 November that ended at government house with a written protest.
The First Palestine Arab Congress met in Jerusalem in January 1919, timed to coincide with the Paris Peace Conference, to submit counter-claims to Zionist claims.

The First Congress (27 January–10 February 1919) had 27 delegates from Muslim-Christian societies, resolved that Palestine was part of Arab Syria and cabled the Peace Conference opposing the Balfour Declaration.

The Third Palestine Arab Congress (Haifa, December 1920) declared the Balfour Declaration null and void, demanded an end to Jewish immigration and chose Musa Kazim al-Husseini as chairman of the Arab Executive Committee it created, a post he held until his death in 1934.

At the December 1920 Congress the MCA framework became the main organisational structure of the national movement, with Musa Kazim al-Husseini as president and Christian vice-presidents Ya'qub Farraj (Jerusalem) and Tawfiq Abdallah (Acre).
Musa Kazim al-Husseini had been dismissed as mayor of Jerusalem in 1920 and replaced by Raghib al-Nashashibi after British authorities accused him of inciting the April 1920 clashes.
Churchill met the Arab Executive in Jerusalem on 28 March 1921.
The Fourth Congress (Jerusalem, 1921) sent a delegation led by Musa Kazim al-Husseini to London to persuade Britain to abandon the Balfour Declaration policy.

A Palestinian Museum Digital Archive photograph identifies the London delegation as Musa Kazim al-Husseini, Tawfiq Hammad, Ibrahim Shammas, Shibli al-Jamal, Amin al-Tamimi and Mu'in al-Madi (the archive dates the photograph 1920).

On 21 February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation (signed by Musa Kazim al-Husseini, President, and Shibly Jamal, Secretary) rejected the draft Order in Council, demanded a 'national independent Government' and said the Balfour Declaration could not be a basis for discussion.

The Colonial Office replied on 1 March 1922 that 'the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge' to the Jewish people, and on 11 April 1922 that there could be 'no question of rescinding the Balfour Declaration'.

The House of Lords passed Lord Islington's motion against acceptance of the Palestine Mandate in June 1922 ('a significant defeat of the Government'), and on 4 July 1922 the Commons voted to support government policy, reported as 292–35.
The Fifth Congress (Nablus, opened 22 August 1922) resolved to reject the new constitution and boycott the Legislative Council elections; the Sixth Congress met in Jaffa in June 1923.

entries.topic: Article 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations and the Palestine Mandate

claims.text: Article 22 paragraph 1 declared that 'the well-being and development of such peoples form a sacred trust of civilisation'.
Paragraph 2 provided that 'the tutelage of such peoples should be entrusted to advanced nations'.

Paragraph 4 stated that communities formerly belonging to the Turkish Empire had reached a stage where 'their existence as independent nations can be provisionally recognised subject to the rendering of administrative advice and assistance by a Mandatory'.
Paragraph 4 also stated: 'The wishes of these communities must be a principal consideration in the selection of the Mandatory.'
Paragraph 7 required each Mandatory to render 'an annual report' to the Council, and paragraph 9 created 'a permanent Commission' to examine those reports.
The League Commission's final report containing Article 22 was approved on 28 April 1919, and the Covenant entered into force on 10 January 1920 with the treaty of peace with Germany.

The 'A' mandates (paragraph 4) were allocated at San Remo on 25 April 1920 and covered Palestine, Trans-Jordan, and Syria and Lebanon, with Iraq also designated 'A' and admitted to the League in 1932; in all, 15 mandates were created over 3 former Ottoman and 7 former German territories.
Britannica lists Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine as Class A mandates and states they all 'achieved full independence by 1949'.
The League of Nations' own 1945 study described the Palestine Mandate as 'of a very special character', following the 'A' framework but adding provisions to carry out the Balfour Declaration.

The UN study 'Origins and Evolution of the Palestine Problem' states that Palestine 'was in no manner excluded' from the class 'A' provisions and that Palestinians were never consulted on the choice of Mandatory.
On 21 February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation invoked Article 22 in demanding a 'national independent Government'.

John Quigley (Britain and Its Mandate over Palestine, Anthem Press, 2022) argues that Article 22 gave the Council no power to distribute territory and that the Zionist-drafted Mandate ignored the population's wishes, a manifest violation of Article 22.

Matthijs de Blois (Israel Law Review 49(3), 2016) argues the Palestine Mandate was unique in naming the Jewish people, wherever they lived, as beneficiaries, and notes Palestinian Arab representatives rejected it as incompatible with self-determination.

disputes.question: Was the Palestine Mandate consistent with Article 22?

positions.view: No: Palestine was an 'A' community whose provisional independence and wishes Article 22 protected; the Mandate's national-home provisions and the absence of consultation departed from it (UN study; Quigley; the 1922 Arab Delegation).

It was a deliberately special mandate: the League itself described it as 'of a very special character' built around the Balfour Declaration, and de Blois argues its specific obligations to the Jewish people are its defining legal feature.
Middle position attributed to Ralph Wilde: Palestine stayed within the Mandates system, and provisions purporting to vary Article 22 had no legal effect.

entries.topic: Amin al-Husseini's appointment as Mufti of Jerusalem (1921) and the Supreme Muslim Council

claims.text: A British military tribunal convicted Amin al-Husseini in absentia after the April 1920 Nebi Musa violence and sentenced him to 10 years' imprisonment; he had fled to Syria.
He was pardoned by High Commissioner Herbert Samuel and returned to Jerusalem later in 1920.
Mufti Kamil al-Husseini, Amin's brother, died on 21 March 1921.
On 12 April 1921 the Muslim electoral body chose three candidates; Amin was not among the top three, and Raghib al-Nashashibi backed Husam al-Din Jarallah.
One account, relying on Joseph Schechtman's The Mufti and the Fuehrer, states Amin placed fourth with 'about 7% of the vote'.
In a note dated 11 April 1921 Samuel recorded meeting Amin, with Storrs present, and Amin's pledge that he and his family would work to keep Jerusalem calm.
Samuel asked Jerusalem governor Ronald Storrs to persuade Raghib al-Nashashibi to drop Jarallah; Jarallah withdrew, which allowed Amin to qualify.
Amin al-Husseini became Mufti of Jerusalem on 8 May 1921.
The Jewish Virtual Library states that British Arabist Ernest Richmond pressed Samuel to appoint him and that Samuel did so with 'some trepidation'.
The USHMM states the British backed him because they accepted his assurances of cooperation and believed only he had the credentials and family connections to keep Palestine calm.

A Muslim conference on Sharia courts and waqf was convened on 9 November 1920; Samuel approved a Regulation on 12 March 1921 (gazetted 15 May 1921); secondary electors met at Government House on 24 August 1921.

The Supreme Moslem Sharia Council Order, issued in Jerusalem on 20 December 1921, created a Council of a Rais al-Ulema plus four members (two for Jerusalem, one each for Nablus and Acre) serving four-year terms.
Under Article 8 the Council was 'to administer and control Moslem Awkaf', nominate Kadis, and appoint Muftis from three candidates chosen by a special electoral college.
Amin al-Husseini became president of the newly established Supreme Muslim Council on 9 January 1922; the Council controlled Sharia courts and waqf funds.

disputes.question: Was the Mufti appointment a manipulation of the election or a normal exercise of government choice?

positions.view: Overrode the vote: Amin was not in the top three (one account says fourth, ~7%); British officials induced Jarallah's withdrawal to make Amin eligible.
Policy choice to secure calm: British officials accepted his assurances and saw him as uniquely able to keep order.
Palestinian biographical account (Walid Khalidi) presents him as succeeding his brother in May 1921, without discussing the election.
August 1920.
Autumn 1920.
'Later in 1920' (no month).

disputes.question: Was he elected or appointed to the Supreme Muslim Council presidency, and for how long?

positions.view: Elected, to a lifelong presidency (COJS).
Appointed president of a council the High Commissioner instituted (Khalidi); the Order itself sets four-year terms.

entries.topic: Nebi Musa 1920, the founding of the Haganah, Jabotinsky's trial, and the end of the Jewish Legion

claims.text: The Jerusalem disturbances began with the Nebi Musa pilgrimage on 4 April 1920 (Easter Day); the military Court of Inquiry (Palin) was convened on 12 April 1920 and reported from Port Said on 1 July 1920 after hearing 152 witnesses.

The Palin report recorded casualties of 5 Jews killed, 18 dangerously wounded and 193 wounded (216 total); 4 Muslims killed, 1 dangerously wounded and 20 wounded (25); 5 Christians and 7 soldiers wounded; 251 overall.

The Court concluded 'the incidence of the attack was against the Jews', called the Balfour Declaration 'the starting point of the whole trouble', and criticised the Zionist Commission's assumption of parallel administrative functions.
The Court found the Jewish self-defence organisers' intention 'purely defensive' and recorded that 'the arrest and prosecution of Mr. Jabotinsky was ungenerous'.
Jabotinsky was arrested with 19 others, mostly former Legionnaires; a military court sentenced him to 15 years' hard labour and his 19 comrades to three years each.

In July 1920 High Commissioner Herbert Samuel amnestied those imprisoned over the Jerusalem riots, Jews and Arabs alike; Jabotinsky left Acre prison and in September 1920 had the sentences quashed in London.
Jabotinsky objected to an amnesty that bracketed defenders with aggressors and pressed until the War Office revoked the sentences.

The Haganah was founded in June 1920, when an Ahdut ha-Avodah conference at Kinneret accepted Ha-Shomer's decision to disband and chose a committee, including Israel Shohat and Eliyahu Golomb, to organise a defence body.

The Histadrut, at its founding convention in December 1920, accepted responsibility for guard and defence matters; in the 1920s Haganah volunteers 'did not exceed a few hundred', armed mainly with revolvers and grenades.

The Jewish battalions numbered over 5,000 men by early 1919; in the second half of 1919 they were cut to one battalion and by spring 1920 'a mere 300 to 400 men remained'; Jabotinsky was forcibly demobilised in August 1919.

On 1 May 1921 the Legion officer Margolin led armed men into Jaffa without military permission, was charged with breach of discipline and forced to resign; the last 400 Palestinian Legionnaires joined a mixed Arab-Jewish militia created by Samuel.

positions.view: Amnestied by Samuel in July 1920, sentences quashed in September 1920 (Schechtman, Encyclopaedia Judaica).
Commuted to one year with banishment from Palestine (Encyclopedia of World Biography, on the same page) — contradicts the EJ account.

disputes.question: Did the Histadrut directly control the Haganah from 1920?

positions.view: Histadrut 'accepted responsibility' for defence matters (Slutsky, EJ).
Haganah was placed under the Histadrut's direct control (Atlas, Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East).
Palin Court: attacks directed mainly against Jews; Jewish organisers defensive.
Palestinian biographical framing (Khalidi): Amin al-Husseini was sentenced 'for having led demonstrations' — political protest for Syrian unity.

entries.topic: The 1922 Legislative Council proposal and the 1923 election boycott

claims.text: The Palestine Order in Council was issued in London on 10 August 1922 and proclaimed in force by Samuel on 1 September 1922.
Article 19 of the Order set the Legislative Council at 22 members plus the High Commissioner: 10 official and 12 unofficial (elected) members; Article 30 set the quorum at ten.
The 12 elected seats were to be 8 Muslim, 2 Christian and 2 Jewish; Philip Mattar notes Palestinian Arabs were allotted 43% of seats while forming 88% of the population.
An earlier draft included 2 nominated members, which the Colonial Office agreed to drop; the Arab Delegation demanded that all members be elected and objected to a quorum of ten.
On 18 June 1922 the Zionist Organisation Executive assured the government its activities 'will be conducted in conformity with the policy therein set forth' in the White Paper.

The Zionist leadership accepted the White Paper without seeing it as a triumph; Weizmann and others believed its 'economic absorptive capacity' principle could still allow a Jewish majority to be built.
The Fifth Palestine Arab Congress (Nablus, August 1922) resolved to boycott the Legislative Council elections.
In the late-February 1923 primary elections no more than 213 of 809 expected secondary electors were chosen; Muslim districts expected to yield 663 produced only 107.

Jews and Druze participated fully; Muslims filled about one-sixth and Christians one-third of their allotments, and even after the polling was extended on 7 March 1923 the result was too unrepresentative to form a council.
Britain then proposed a nominated Advisory Council with Arab, Jewish and Christian members; the Arab nominees refused their seats and the idea collapsed.

An 'Arab Agency' analogous to the Jewish Agency, but with members chosen by the High Commissioner, was offered and rejected in October 1923; the Arab Executive's president wrote that the Arabs' 'sole object is independence'.
The Mandatory's 1923 report to the League lists a November 1923 White Paper on the 'Proposed Formation of an Arab Agency' and 'Papers relating to the Elections for the Palestine Legislative Council'.
By the end of 1923 Britain governed with an advisory council of British officials only; the High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate.

Later proposals came in 1930 (Passfield) and 1935, when a 28-member council (14 Muslims and Christians, 8 Jews, 5 officials, 1 commercial member) was suspended amid Jewish opposition and Arab division; the idea died with the 1936–39 revolt.

disputes.question: Why did the Zionist side accept and the Arab side reject the 1922 constitution?

positions.view: Arab leadership: the council was built on the Mandate and Balfour Declaration, gave Arabs a minority of seats despite being the large majority, and fell short of a national government with control of immigration.
Zionist leadership: accepted the White Paper and council because the framework kept the national-home commitment and immigration tied to economic capacity rather than Arab consent.

claims.text: The Jewish Agency puts the Third Aliyah (1919–1923) at about 35,000 immigrants, 53% from Russia and 36% from Poland, with about 800 from Western and Central Europe.
The Jewish Virtual Library puts it at approximately 40,000 and says the yishuv numbered about 90,000 by the end of the period.
Many Third Aliyah immigrants were graduates of He-Halutz in Russia and Poland and of Ha-Shomer ha-Tsa'ir in Galicia; they founded the Histadrut and played a leading role in creating the Haganah.
The UN study records Jewish immigration of 5,514 (part-year 1920), 9,149 (1921), 7,844 (1922) and 7,421 (1923), against 202, 190, 284 and 570 non-Jewish immigrants.
The Mandatory's 1922 report records 8,128 immigrants in 1922, 'of these 7,844 were Jews', and emigration of 2,939.
The October 1922 census counted 757,182 people: 590,890 Muslims, 83,794 Jews and 73,024 Christians.
In 1920 the Zionist Organization was permitted a quota of 16,500 immigrants per year (COJS describes them as heads of household) under conditions of self-support, health and a passport.
On 15 May 1921, after the Jaffa riots, Samuel temporarily prohibited Jewish immigration, including about 150 immigrants already en route.
In his 3 June 1921 speech Samuel tied future Jewish immigration to the country's economic capacity; the 1922 White Paper said immigration must not exceed 'economic capacity to absorb new arrivals'.
Gedud ha-Avodah (the Labour Legion) was founded in autumn 1920 by 80 Third Aliyah pioneers who were disciples of Joseph Trumpeldor, starting with a contract on the Tiberias–Tabgha road.
Gedud ha-Avodah founded Ein Harod in 1921 and Tel Yosef in 1923, peaked at about 700 members, and more than 2,000 pioneers passed through it before it split in 1923 and 1926.
Degania, called the first kibbutz, was founded on 28 October 1910, during the Second Aliyah and before the Third.
The Histadrut was founded at a convention in December 1920.
Jewish land purchases were recorded at about 100,000 dunams in 1921, 45,000 in 1922 and 34,440 in 1923.

entries.topic: Sharif Hussein of Mecca after the war: Versailles, the mandates and the failed Anglo-Hejazi treaty

claims.text: In 1919 Hussein declined to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, in protest at the mandates imposed on Syria, Palestine and Iraq; his son Faisal represented him in Paris.
Hussein refused to recognise the Paris settlements and refused to ratify the Anglo-Hashemite treaty, which cost him British support when Ibn Saud invaded.
British India Office file IOR/L/PS/10/881 (25 May 1921–25 August 1925) documents the subsidy question and negotiations for an Anglo-Hejazi treaty.
On 28 November 1921 T. E. Lawrence telegraphed the Colonial Secretary proposing to revise draft Article 4 so as to 'clear away all agreements' Hussein cited but could not produce.
A treaty text was signed by Lawrence and Emir Abdullah in December 1921, and Hussein threatened to abdicate on 27 February 1922.
The Foreign Office considered requiring Hussein to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and accept the British treaty before inviting him to Britain.

On 19 April 1923 Curzon sent Jeddah a revised draft initialled by himself and Hussein's agent Dr Naji al-Asil, differing chiefly in a new Article 2 and in Articles 3–5 on 'the disputed land frontiers of the Hedjaz'.
Instead of a continuing subsidy, Britain offered Hussein a single final payment of £50,000.
Jordan's official Arab Revolt centennial site states Hussein refused the 1921 treaty because it required him to recognise the mandate over Palestine and with it a Jewish national home.
Hussein proclaimed himself caliph in March 1924, was caught unprepared by an Ikhwan attack on Taif in September 1924, and abdicated on 5 October 1924.
After the abdication Britain refused further treaty negotiations with his son King Ali 'so long as present unsettled conditions in the Hejaz continue'.
Hussein lived in exile in Cyprus until 1930 and died in Amman in 1931 (3 June 1931 per the Jordanian site, which says he was buried at the al-Aqsa compound).
The 1922 Churchill White Paper statement held that 'the whole of Palestine west of the Jordan was thus excluded from Sir H. McMahon's pledge'.
The Palestine Arab Delegation replied that McMahon used 'districts', not 'vilayet', that the reservation meant Lebanon, and that 'Palestine thus comes within the scope of the promise'.

disputes.question: Did Britain keep its wartime promises to Hussein, and what does his refusal show?

positions.view: Promises kept: Lawrence wrote the Cairo settlement was 'fulfilling (I think) our promises in letter and spirit', and in January 1921 told Churchill Faisal had agreed to 'abandon all claims of his father to Palestine'.

Promises broken: the Hashemite account says 'the Allies did not keep their promises', and Hussein's refusal to sign a treaty recognising the Palestine mandate reflects that view; the Arab Delegation held Palestine was inside McMahon's pledge.
British official position: Palestine west of the Jordan was always excluded from the McMahon pledge.

entries.topic: The Mandate for Palestine (1922–1923) and the Transjordan memorandum

claims.text: The Mandate text ends 'Done at London the twenty-fourth day of July, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two.'
Article 1 gave the Mandatory 'full powers of legislation and of administration'.

Article 2 made the Mandatory responsible for conditions securing the Jewish national home and the development of self-governing institutions, and for 'safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine'.

Article 4 provided that 'an appropriate Jewish agency shall be recognized as a public body' to advise the Administration, and recognised the Zionist Organization as that agency while its constitution was deemed appropriate.

Article 6 required the Administration to 'facilitate Jewish immigration under suitable conditions' and encourage close settlement by Jews on the land, while ensuring that other sections of the population are not prejudiced.
Article 11 allowed public ownership or control of natural resources and public works, and allowed arrangements with the Jewish agency for such works, with distributed profits capped.
Article 22 made English, Arabic and Hebrew the official languages, with Arabic inscriptions on stamps or money repeated in Hebrew and vice versa.

Article 25 let the Mandatory, with Council consent, postpone or withhold provisions in the territories between the Jordan and Palestine's eastern boundary, but not in conflict with Articles 15, 16 and 18.
In July 1922 the Council approved the terms of the Syria and Palestine mandates conditionally, pending a France–Italy agreement on Syria.
At its Geneva meeting of 29 September 1923 the Council took note that, the France–Italy agreement having been reported, the two mandates had 'automatically and simultaneously entered into force'.
On 16 September 1922 the Council approved a British memorandum under Article 25 declaring that listed provisions 'are not applicable to the territory known as Transjordan'.

The excluded provisions were Preamble recitals 2 and 3, part of Article 2, Articles 4 and 6, part of Article 7 (on Palestinian citizenship for Jews), part of Article 11, and Articles 13, 14, 22 and 23; Britain accepted 'full responsibility as Mandatory for Transjordan'.
The League later noted that the Zionist Organisation was replaced in 1929 by the 'Jewish Agency for Palestine' as the Article 4 agency.

disputes.question: Did the Mandate validly enter into force on 29 September 1923?

positions.view: Yes: League record C.L.101.1923.VI states the mandates had automatically and simultaneously entered into force at that meeting, and the UN later used that date.

No (John Quigley, 2026): the Council only 'noted', in the future tense, that the mandates would enter into force; Secretary-General Drummond's circular changed the tense; Britain lacked title because the Treaty of Lausanne (signed 24 July 1923) entered into force only on 6 August 1924.

entries.topic: Allenby's entry into Jerusalem (1917) and Ronald Storrs as governor (1917–1926)

claims.text: On 9 December 1917 Jerusalem's mayor Hussein al-Husayni tried to surrender the city first to two British cooks and then to two scout sergeants before Colonel Watson accepted the letter of surrender.
General Allenby arrived two days later, dismounted at Jaffa Gate and entered the city on foot; the mayor, citing pneumonia, missed the official ceremony and died a few weeks later.
Allenby's proclamation of 11 December 1917 was addressed 'To the Inhabitants of Jerusalem the Blessed and the People Dwelling in Its Vicinity' and placed the city under martial law.

The proclamation said 'every person pursue his lawful business without fear of interruption' and that holy places would be protected 'according to the existing customs and beliefs of those to whose faith they are sacred'.
The proclamation was read at the citadel inside Jaffa Gate and issued in seven languages.
Jewish residents saw the conquest, a month after the Balfour Declaration, as a 'Hanukkah miracle'; parts of the Christian world hailed it as a 'Christmas gift'.

Writing in Al Jazeera (2014), Hatem Bazian argues that 11 December 1917 made Jerusalem occupied territory and began a colonial project that enabled Zionism; he cites a 'crusades' remark that Allenby 'reportedly' made, without a primary source.

Ronald Storrs was Military Governor of Jerusalem from 1917 to 1920 and Civil Governor of Jerusalem and Judea from 1920 to 1926, then Governor of Cyprus (1926) and Northern Rhodesia (1933–34); his papers are at Pembroke College, Cambridge.

The Pro-Jerusalem Society's records state it was 'Founded September 1918. Incorporated October 1920'; its council included the Mayor, the Director of Antiquities and the Grand Mufti, with Storrs as President and Samuel as Honorary President.

A public notice under Storrs required a written permit from the Military Governor to build, alter or repair within 2,500 metres of the Damascus Gate, and forbade 'the use of stucco and corrugated iron within the ancient city walls'.
The Society reopened the original tile kilns in the Haram al-Sharif area for Dome of the Rock repairs and contracted the Armenian potter David Ohanessian.

Historian Mahon Murphy notes the Society restored the Citadel with refugee labour and removed the clock tower over Jaffa Gate, and argues its multi-faith council was subordinate to Storrs's biblical vision.
A 2022 Exeter PhD thesis (C. Burnham) argues Storrs governed Jerusalem in a deeply personal, Orientalist way, constrained by his superiors, Palestinians and the Zionist movement.
An Israeli design curator credited Storrs's requirement that buildings be faced in Jerusalem stone, which 'still exist[s] today', and praised his preservation approach.

positions.view: Liberation: Jewish (and many Christian) contemporaries celebrated it as deliverance from Ottoman rule.
Occupation: Palestinian-perspective writers mark it as the start of British colonial rule that enabled the Zionist project.
Preservationist steward of a multi-faith city (Israeli curators, Media Line report).
Personal and Orientalist rule that subordinated local voices to a British biblical vision (Murphy; Burnham).
